lesson.title: Antipsychotic Medications: Managing Symptoms, Not Defining a Person
lesson.summary: Antipsychotic medications reduce symptoms of psychosis, such as hallucinations and delusions, most often associated with schizophrenia, largely by acting on dopamine activity in the brain, though how they work has grown more nuanced as newer medications have been developed.
lesson.body:
Antipsychotic medications are most commonly used to treat symptoms of psychosis, such as hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking, in people diagnosed with schizophrenia and certain other conditions.

For decades, researchers have observed a connection between overactivity in certain dopamine pathways in the brain and psychotic symptoms, an idea sometimes called the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia. Most antipsychotic medications reduce dopamine activity at specific receptors as part of how they relieve these symptoms. This hypothesis has been an influential starting point for both research and treatment, but researchers now generally view it as an incomplete picture. Other neurotransmitter systems and brain circuits also appear to be involved, and the full picture of how psychosis develops is still being actively studied.

Earlier antipsychotic medications, sometimes called first-generation or typical antipsychotics, were developed starting in the 1950s and act mainly on dopamine receptors. Newer second-generation, or atypical, antipsychotics were developed later and act on a broader range of receptors, including some serotonin receptors. These newer medications were developed in part to reduce certain movement-related side effects that were more commonly associated with earlier medications. Which type of medication is a better fit varies from person to person, and that decision is made by a treating clinician, not something covered by this chapter.

The development of early antipsychotic medications is often cited, alongside broader shifts in mental health policy, as one of the developments that contributed to the historical move away from long-term psychiatric institutionalization in many countries during the mid-twentieth century.

Schizophrenia and the medications used to treat it are often surrounded by public misunderstanding and stigma. Understanding these medications as tools that treat specific symptoms, not as something that changes who a person fundamentally is, is an important part of engaging with this topic respectfully and accurately.
